stem: Match the coronary artery to the location of infarction
answer:
The pairings:

Coronary arteryLocation of infarction
Left Anterior Descending ArteryAnterior MI
Right Coronary ArteryInferior MI
Left Circumflex ArteryPosterior MI

From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The culprit artery sets the wall that infarcts:

  • LAD - anterior MI: ST elevation in the anterior leads V3-V4 (V1-V6 if it extends septal and lateral). The LAD supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum.
  • RCA - inferior MI: ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. In the 85% who are right-dominant, the RCA gives the posterior descending artery.
  • Left circumflex - posterior MI: often missed on a 12-lead. Look for ST depression in V1-V3 or add V8-V9.

stem: Match the muscle of the larynx with its function.
answer:
The pairings:

MuscleFunction
Cricothyroid muscleLengthens the vocal cords
Vocalis muscleShortens the vocal cords
Posterior cricoarytenoid muscleAbducts the vocal cords
Lateral cricoarytenoid musclePivot-adducts the vocal cords
Interarytenoid muscleTranslational-adducts the vocal cords
Aryepiglottic musclePulls epiglottis down

From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Each muscle acts on either the cricothyroid joint (pitch) or the cricoarytenoid joint (opening and closing):

  • Cricothyroid: cricothyroid tilts the cricothyroid joint to lengthen the cords (↑ pitch). It is the only one supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
  • Vocalis: vocalis/thyroarytenoid shorten the cords (↓ pitch).
  • Posterior cricoarytenoid: posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally. It is the only abductor.
  • Lateral cricoarytenoid: lateral cricoarytenoid rotates them medially, a pivot adduction.
  • Interarytenoid: interarytenoid slides the arytenoids together, a translational adduction synergistic with the lateral cricoarytenoid.
  • Aryepiglottic: aryepiglottic pulls the epiglottis down to close the inlet in swallowing.

stem: Match each of the following to either ALT > AST or AST > ALT.
answer:
The pairings:

ConditionEnzyme pattern
NAFLDALT > AST
Acute Budd-Chiari syndromeAST > ALT
Alcoholic liver diseaseAST > ALT
Viral hepatitisALT > AST
Celiac diseaseALT > AST
Ischemic hepatitisAST > ALT

From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. AST is found outside the liver (muscle, red cells, brain) and falls in mitochondria-heavy, alcoholic, ischemic or vascular injury; ALT is the more liver-specific enzyme and dominates in most inflammatory or metabolic hepatocellular injury. The lecture's lists sort each item:

  • NAFLD = ALT > AST: steatosis and NASH are ALT-predominant.
  • Acute Budd-Chiari = AST > ALT: hepatic venous outflow obstruction behaves like ischemic or congestive injury.
  • Alcoholic liver disease = AST > ALT: classically at 2:1 or more.
  • Viral hepatitis = ALT > AST: acute or chronic.
  • Celiac disease = ALT > AST: a systemic cause of mild ALT elevation.
  • Ischemic hepatitis = AST > ALT, grouped with congestive hepatopathy.
